newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE coffee finishes higher after switchback ride.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE coffee finishes higher after switchback ride.

text.p: LIFFE coffee futures ended Monday slightly higher after a choppy session dominated by nearby spread activity.

May and July positions formed the bulk of the the day's modest volume of 3,851 lots, with the May/July switches trading at $15-$18 at one stage. The May discount to July narrowed to $10 by the close, the same as Friday's finish.
By the close, May stood $6 higher at $1,575 after a intraday low of $1,545. It had touched a high of $1,595 and partially filled a chart gap at $1,590-$1,610.
Pending further news, the market could be confined to a range between $1,500 and $1,600 a tonne basis May. Last week's fund long liquidation seemed to have abated for now.
However a forecast of lower Indonesian 1997 coffee exports did little to move the market.
"The market believes that there's good supply of robustas and the possible Indonesian shortfall is not particulary worrisome," said one trader.

In the medium term, traders will be keeping a close eye on Brazilian weather. Some had turned jittery after news the first frosts of the year in Brazil over the weekend, some 15 days earlier than usual.

But there had been no threat of frost in coffee areas and according to some records, the earliest frosts to hit the coffee belts in the last 100 years was on May 31, with the key months June and July.

"With the global coffee stocks so low, the first frost of the year in the south of the country has started to focus minds on what could happen should a cold snap devastate coffee regions as it did in 1994," broker GNI said.
Earlier Indonesian exporters forecast 1997 coffee production some 30 percent short of an originally forecast 480,000 tonnes, due to bad weather.

"Surveys done by exporters showed that incessant rains in 1996 and strong winds in coffee-growing areas in Sumatra had affected the fruiting process resulting in a decline in coffee production," said Osman Soedargo, head of the exporter group.
He said results of the survey were received three days ago and exportable volume would amount to some 220,000 tonnes this year compared with about 300,000 tonnes in 1996.

Elsewhere, Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi signalled that the country's state-run coffee export auction system would remain unchanged despite pressure for a bigger role by private millers. -- Jalil Hamid, London newsroom +44 171 542 4985
